c.tagline: A maze of souks, spice, and rooftop sunsets.

avoid.reason: No true no-go zones, but skip the unlit outer medina alleys and the Sidi Youssef Ben Ali fringe late at night, when getting lost invites hassle.
Jemaa el-Fnaa and the souks see pickpocketing, aggressive touts, henna-scam artists and 'false guide' scams, especially after dark.

hood_desc: The ancient walled old city, a maze of souks, riads, palaces and the famous Jemaa el-Fna square alive with performers and food stalls. Ideal for travelers who want to immerse themselves in traditional Marrakech, sights and sensory bustle.

The modern French-built district with wide boulevards, contemporary cafes, boutiques, galleries and a lively dining scene. Suits visitors wanting a more relaxed, cosmopolitan base with modern comforts.
An upmarket quarter of luxury hotels, gardens, nightclubs and casinos between the old and new towns. Best for travelers seeking upscale accommodation and nightlife close to the medina.

The historic southern part of the medina around the royal palaces and the Saadian Tombs, quieter and rich in monuments. Good for those wanting history and atmosphere with fewer crowds than the central souks.

A tranquil palm-grove district on the city's outskirts, dotted with luxury villas, resorts and spas among the palms. Perfect for travelers wanting a peaceful, resort-style retreat away from the medina bustle.
lodging: Radisson Blu Hotel Marrakech Carre Eden

water.note: Officially treated but CDC/NHS advise visitors stick to bottled or filtered water.

transit.pay: City buses are run by ALSA; pay the driver in cash, about 5 MAD (~US$0.50) per ride, so carry small change. There is no transit card worth getting for a short visit. Airport bus L19 sells tickets on board (30 MAD, ~US$3).
transit.hours: Buses run roughly 6am-10pm; there is no night service.
transit.note: Most visitors walk the medina and use petit taxis (insist on the meter or agree a price first); buses mainly help for Gueliz, the Palmeraie and the airport.
